title: Short Stuff: Dangers of Nose Picking
summary: Short Stuff episode warning listeners against nose picking. Josh and Chuck open by linking the nose and brain: a sudden loss of smell can be an early warning sign of dementia or Alzheimer's, per University of Chicago Medicine research. They then discuss a Brisbane, Australia study (QIMR Berghofer-style neurobiology research, named in transcript as the Clem Jones Center for Neurobiology and Stem Cell Research) using mouse models, which found that Chlamydia pneumoniae can travel from the nose to the brain and trigger amyloid plaque production, with the bacterium also linked speculatively to multiple sclerosis, asthma, and cardiovascular problems. The hosts say picking the nose can push such bacteria toward the brain. Next they cover a Madison, Wisconsin survey of 254 respondents in which nearly all reported picking their nose, with response bias caveats; about 2 percent picked obsessively, with cases of septum perforation; researchers suggested compulsive nose picking (rhinotillexomania) should not be classed as a mental disorder. They discuss nose hair trimming, a 2000 Bangalore, India study finding nose picking is more common in adults than teenagers, social acceptability differences (US, Japan, China with air pollution), and close with a light sign-off.
topics: loss of smell and dementia risk

segments.title: Intro and nose-brain link
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on dangers of nose picking and credit a listener's wife. They explain that a sudden loss of smell may be an early warning sign of dementia or Alzheimer's, citing University of Chicago Medicine research.
topics: loss of smell and dementia risk

segments.title: Chlamydia pneumoniae from nose to brain
segments.summary: Research from Brisbane, Australia, using mouse models, found Chlamydia pneumoniae can travel from the nose to the brain and trigger amyloid plaque. The hosts discuss the bacterium's possible links to multiple sclerosis, asthma, and cardiovascular problems, and say picking the nose can push bacteria toward the brain.

segments.title: Prevalence of nose picking surveys
segments.summary: A Madison, Wisconsin survey of 254 respondents found nearly everyone who responded reported picking their nose. The hosts note response bias. About 2 percent picked obsessively, with some reporting major damage such as septum perforation. Researchers suggested compulsive nose picking, rhinotillexomania, be dropped as a mental disorder label.

segments.title: Nose hair, age, and social norms
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss trimming nose hair and a 2000 Bangalore, India study that found nose picking more common in adults than teenagers. They then compare social acceptance of nose picking in the US, Japan, and China, including air pollution as a reason for picking in China.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts joke about admitting to picking their noses and close the episode.
